label: Symplectic Capacities
notes: This chapter, printed pages 457 to 502, introduces capacities as numerical obstructions to symplectic embeddings. We motivate them through Gromov nonsqueezing, then build toward rigidity, the Hofer metric, the Hofer-Zehnder capacity, and a variational construction that ties the dynamic and embedding viewpoints together throughout the lecture.

label: What a Capacity Measures
notes: A capacity assigns one positive number to every symplectic manifold in a fixed dimension. The number behaves like an area: it is monotone under embeddings, scales by lambda squared under conformal rescaling of the form, and is pinned by a normalization on the ball and the cylinder.

label: The Capacity Axioms
notes: Three axioms govern every capacity. Monotonicity forbids large objects from embedding into small ones, conformality fixes how capacity reacts to scaling the form, and normalization gives the shared value pi r squared on the unit ball and the standard cylinder. Together they make capacity an honest symplectic invariant.

label: Gromov Nonsqueezing
notes: Gromov nonsqueezing is the founding theorem of the subject. A symplectic embedding of the radius r ball into the cylinder of radius R can exist only when r is at most R. Volume places no such limit, so the obstruction is genuinely symplectic and not measure theoretic at all.

label: Ball Versus Cylinder
notes: This diagram is the heart of the chapter. The ball wants to enter the cylinder, but its radial shadow on the symplectic two plane is trapped by the cylinder radius. The obstruction r at most R is visible geometrically, while the infinite length of the cylinder makes volume comparison useless.

label: Why Volume Is Too Weak
notes: The cylinder has infinite volume, so any ball fits inside by sheer measure. Yet nonsqueezing forbids the embedding once r exceeds R. The capacity bar chart records exactly this gap: volume permits the map while the capacity inequality detects the obstruction the volume comparison cannot see.

label: The Gromov Width
notes: The Gromov width is the first and smallest capacity. It equals the area pi r squared of the largest ball that embeds symplectically into the manifold. Nonsqueezing is precisely the statement that this width is finite and bounded by the cylinder, giving the capacity axioms a concrete model.

label: Symplectic Rigidity
notes: Capacities expose symplectic rigidity. A volume preserving map can deform a ball into any equal volume shape, but a symplectomorphism must respect every capacity. The group of symplectic maps is therefore closed inside the volume preserving group, a closure phenomenon that no purely measure theoretic argument could ever produce.

label: The Hofer-Zehnder Capacity
notes: The Hofer-Zehnder capacity is built from Hamiltonian dynamics. One takes admissible Hamiltonians supported in the manifold whose flows carry no fast periodic orbits, and the capacity is the supremum of their oscillation. Finiteness of this number forces the existence of a short closed orbit, linking embeddings to dynamics.

label: The Hofer Metric
notes: The Hofer norm measures a Hamiltonian by the time integral of its oscillation, the maximum minus the minimum over the manifold. This yields a bi-invariant distance on the group of compactly supported Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms. Its nondegeneracy, that the identity sits at positive distance from nearby maps, is deep and rigidity driven.

label: Variational Construction
notes: Capacities arise variationally from the symplectic action functional on loops. Critical points are periodic orbits, and a minimax over a suitable family of loops selects a distinguished action value. That value satisfies the capacity axioms, so the embedding obstruction and the dynamical orbit emerge from one variational principle.

label: Capacity Toolbox
notes: We collect the working facts. Capacity is monotone and conformal, equals pi r squared on balls and cylinders, scales quadratically with radius while volume scales with the full dimension, and detects rigidity that volume misses. These properties make capacity the standard numerical certificate against symplectic embeddings.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We have turned an abstract symplectic claim into a finite testable invariant. Nonsqueezing, the Gromov width, Hofer-Zehnder, and the Hofer metric all detect the same rigidity from embedding and dynamical sides. The next chapters push capacities toward global existence results, fixed point counts, and open embedding problems.
